name: Nora Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead legal-aid scheduling software at a tech company, where I am among the best at tracing lost appointments. I use AI occasionally to understand old code, but check dates with a clerk. Fadi repairs appliances, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with four months of expenses saved and some similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the legal-aid scheduling team that a little AI help can catch a duplicate hearing date, but a client still needs the right room and time. I use AI occasionally to explain legacy code and check it against the case calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead the software team at a tech company serving legal-aid offices. I am good at tracing a lost appointment; Fadi repairs appliances, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has left us renting with four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing one mismatched hearing list with the legal-aid clerk each Monday. We would save 140 monthly while both incomes hold and repair our old wardrobe before buying another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our jobs and rent here. A wrong hearing date is a missed chance to be heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong in a hearing list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client had a morning date in the email and an afternoon date in the office calendar. I found the mismatch before the clerk sent the reminder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check with the clerk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clerk knows whether the court changed a room by telephone. A code test cannot hear a call that was never entered.

say: I want **hearing dates** checked with a legal-aid clerk.
I use **AI occasionally** for code explanations, then verify calendars.
think: I have **four months saved** from typical lead pay and Fadi’s appliance repairs.
I see **rent covered** while both current household incomes continue.
do: **Review hearing mismatches** with clerk every Monday.
**Save 140 monthly** while both incomes hold; repair wardrobe rather than replace it.

fieldNote: Her **lead skill** lies in finding scheduling errors before clients lose access.
Four months saved and **two incomes** support present stability without assuming grown children will help.

Save 140 monthly while developer pay and appliance-repair income continue
Repair old wardrobe instead of buying a replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking writing, booking, checking and coding could shrink the hearing team. The staff association should ask who a client can call when the automated date is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead hours could fall if one engineer oversees many automated calendars. Four months saved gives us some room, but Fadi’s repair income alone will not pay all the rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the association meeting this month to ask for written funded hours and a human correction route for clients. If my hours fall, I’d search paid local legal-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills; I’d keep reviewing the clerk’s mismatch list while employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own pay and the client who cannot reach a person. An appeal that arrives after the hearing is no appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would request funded lead hours and a named clerk to correct a date before a hearing. I would join the group request, not speak for everyone by myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on Fadi working longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if appliance customers book and pay him. We would not put a hoped-for repair job into next month’s rent.

I want **human date correction** for legal-aid clients who receive a wrong hearing time.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** if one engineer oversees several automated offices.
I cannot use **Fadi’s repair income** alone to cover rent and household bills.
do: **Join association meeting** for written hours and client correction route.

**Keep reviewing mismatch list** while current lead role pays.

fieldNote: Her **collective request** seeks paid staffing and a named route for correcting dates.
The **local job search** starts only after reduced hours and a real bill-covering vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write hearing code and handle legal-aid bookings cheaper than our team. Robots repairing appliances and moving court files may arrive around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer role could end even if I know this system better than most. Four months saved would let us search briefly, but Fadi’s appliance work cannot replace my whole wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d delay the planned kitchen repaint and request written notice of any lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local court-record vacancies only if I meet their requirements, openings exist and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office which temporary support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the wage that carries our rent. A court file cannot argue for my next pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would court records work survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would take only an actual paid opening and keep looking if it shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a court job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search nearby offices and software firms first. Fadi’s appliance customers and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach hearing code first.
I expect **physical robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead wage** could end quickly.
I know **four months saved** is a short search buffer.
do: **Delay kitchen repaint** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for court-record vacancies** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: A court file cannot argue for my next pay cheque.
fieldNote: Her **court-record option** remains exposed to AGI and requires a qualified paid opening.
She checks **actual public eligibility** rather than assuming a benefit replaces income.

steps.text: Delay planned kitchen repaint and request written lead-cut notice now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives offices time to trace how a wrong hearing date is corrected before the code changes. Robots moving court files may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the case-office side of corrections while earning my developer wage, though AGI may process much of it too. I would need approved paid access because real case details are private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the legal-aid office and my employer for a paid monthly session to trace one anonymized date correction with a case clerk. If both approve and the office funds the clerk’s time, I’d practise documenting the change; we would save 120 monthly while both incomes hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local case-record vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the lead role but glad to test the office work carefully. The date a client sees must be the date the court expects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you document?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the court notice, office calendar and client reminder with names removed. The clerk would check the corrected record before any real case changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid access is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer job and read public procedure notes. I would not claim a refused visit taught me casework.

say: I want **case correction practice** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **file robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **office corrections** with a case clerk on approved paid time.
I cannot assume **a case-record vacancy** exists or pays our rent.
do: **Trace monthly anonymized corrections** only with both employers approving paid time and funded clerk review; otherwise use public notes.
**Apply for case-record vacancies** after 2031 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but careful** with private case details.
S3.quote: The date a client sees must be the date the court expects.
fieldNote: The **case session** needs two approvals, paid time, anonymized records and funded clerk review.
The **future job** depends on qualification, actual paid local vacancies and bill-covering wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives clients and staff time to make date corrections traceable. Robots moving physical court files may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still work at 68, and I have not checked a retirement amount. Four months saved makes our current rent secure, but a later case-office job cannot be counted before a vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading hearing code and join the association’s annual review of funded hours and human client contact. We would save 130 monthly while both incomes hold and request a written retirement-income estimate; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local case-record vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work but secure in the next few years. A written correction path is more useful than a promise that nobody will make a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for the number of funded developer hours and the person who corrects a disputed date. I would want the answer shared with staff and clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help you stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. Fadi and I will make that decision from verified income and our real bills, not their wages.

I expect **file robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written figure.
I see **current rent secure** with four months saved.
do: **Keep leading hearing code** and join annual association review.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before a qualified paid local records vacancy appears. Written notice, a real bill-covering opening and verified temporary public help would let us use savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a client can simply show up for the next date. A missed hearing may take away a legal-aid client’s only chance to speak.

headlineQuote: A missed hearing may take away a legal-aid client’s only chance to speak.

She seeks **group staffing figures** and takes case-record learning only with paid approved access.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead wage before a paid qualified local opening appears.
